stories.title: Claude chatbot maker Anthropic set for $1.3tn stock market debut
stories.deck: Anthropic has priced its Nasdaq flotation range at $70 to $78 a share, a deal that could raise up to $64bn despite jittery markets.
summary: Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, has set out terms for its stock market debut. In an updated filing reported on Tuesday 10 November, it said it would offer shares at $70 to $78 each. The BBC says that implies a valuation of $1.1tn to $1.3tn and that the company will list on Nasdaq under the symbol ANT on 19 November, becoming the first fully AI-focused company to go public. TechCrunch, on a fully diluted basis at the top of the range, says $1.404tn, so the figure depends on how it is counted. Either way, it is below the $2tn backers reportedly hoped for, though above May's $965bn.

The sale covers 825 million Class A shares and is expected to raise between $57.75bn and $64.35bn. Separately, Anthropic has agreed to sell $26bn of non-voting Class N stock privately to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC, with Google and Nvidia putting in $10bn each. Net proceeds are estimated at $84.6bn to $93.7bn, the higher figure if underwriters use their option to buy extra shares.

The filing also shows what the seven co-founders stand to make. Each plans to sell 3,378,378 shares, which TechCrunch values at about $236m at $70, just under $250m at $74 and about $264m at $78. Afterwards each will hold about 3.2% of Class A shares, around 22% together, though their share of total equity is smaller because Amazon and Google hold non-voting stock. A special Class F share still gives the founders about half the votes, and a trust elects a board majority.

The timing is awkward. The BBC reports the Nasdaq fell sharply after last week's US midterm elections on fears a Democrat-led Congress could slow AI development, amid doubts over whether AI spending will pay off. Anthropic's revenue for the six months to June rose to $16.2bn from $1.1bn a year earlier, but its pre-tax loss grew to $80.7bn from $12.9bn. Analyst Fiona Cincotta told Reuters the $64bn target looks "fairly bullish". The company has also warned that advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" without safeguards.

stories.title: Oura to acquire Counsel Health for $625M
stories.deck: The smart ring maker is buying the AI-driven primary care startup whose chatbot already runs inside its app.
summary: Oura, the smart ring maker, said on Tuesday 10 November that it has agreed to buy Counsel Health for $625 million. Counsel pairs a chat-based medical assistant with access to licensed physicians, and was added to the Oura app in June, according to TechCrunch.

According to The Verge, citing Bloomberg, Oura chief executive Tom Hale sees it as a way to link wearables, clinical AI and doctors, so biometric data informs medical answers. The companies plan to focus on preventative, acute, and specialty and chronic care. Counsel's chief executive, Muthu Alagappan, will become Oura's chief clinical AI officer, and Counsel's 70 employees will join Oura. Its network of on-demand physicians, about 50 people, is also set to grow. Counsel will keep serving enterprise partners such as health plans and employers.
The reports differ on timing. The Verge says Oura expects the deal to close before the end of the year, while TechCrunch says before the end of 2027, so the date is unclear.

Oura announced the deal alongside its quarterly results. TechCrunch reports revenue rose 153% from a year earlier to $533 million for the quarter ended 30 September, and that Oura had postponed an IPO of up to $2.2 billion a few weeks ago, citing uncertainty in the IPO market.

stories.title: OpenAI, Anthropic face new oversight as New York's AI safety law takes effect
stories.deck: The state has opened a registration portal for large AI developers ahead of the RAISE Act's start on 1 January.
summary: New York opened a registration portal on Tuesday 10 November for large frontier AI developers, including OpenAI and Anthropic, which must register by 1 January 2027. The RAISE Act, the state's AI safety and transparency law, takes effect at the start of the year, according to TechCrunch.

The law applies to developers with more than $500 million in annual revenue. They must publish safety frameworks on their websites, report critical safety incidents within 72 hours and issue public transparency reports on their models. A newly formed state body, the Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust, known as DIGIT, will oversee compliance. Penalties can reach $1 million for a first violation and $3 million for later ones.

Governor Kathy Hochul said technology leaders insist their vision for AI is inevitable whatever the collateral damage. She called the state's approach "a national model for smart, sensible AI regulation." She also launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University, which will independently evaluate advanced AI systems and help DIGIT review companies' safety frameworks.

TechCrunch notes other states have similar rules: California's SB 53, in force since January, requires incident reports within 15 days, and Illinois' SB 315 starts in 2027 and adds independent audits.

stories.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy: what is reported
stories.deck: Nvidia has hired a law firm to investigate while Huang, Beijing and the White House give differing accounts of the affair.
summary: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has admitted to a relationship outside his marriage with Alice Huang, who is not related to him. The BBC reports that she is alleged to be a spy for Beijing and is an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore company that has bought from Nvidia. According to a New York Times report cited by the BBC, US intelligence officials believe she spied for Beijing. These claims are not independently confirmed here.

On Tuesday 10 November Nvidia said the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, led by former federal prosecutor Joon Kim, would run "a thorough and independent investigation." Nvidia said it has no reason to believe its secrets were compromised. President Donald Trump said the FBI is looking into the matter, and that Huang told him he "had no idea she was a spy", adding "I really believe him." The FBI declined to comment to the BBC. China's foreign ministry called the allegations "entirely groundless".
Nvidia shares fell more than 4% on Monday, about $250bn off its value, and a proposed California class action accuses the company of concealing Huang's ties.

The Verge says there is no public evidence that Huang directed chips to China or leaked sensitive information. Citing The Information, it reports that companies linked to Alice Huang enabled at least $7 billion of Nvidia chip sales to China. Experts told The Verge the scandal could distract Nvidia.

stories.title: Google's two new specialized TPUs
stories.deck: The chips, built on its eighth-generation design, target confidential AI workloads and larger memory needs.
summary: Google on Monday 9 November unveiled two new versions of its tensor processing units, the in-house chips it designs for AI work. TechCrunch reports the move is part of Google's effort to rely less on chips made by other companies for its cloud business. Both belong to the eighth generation first introduced in April.

The TPU 8tx, designed with AMD, is based on the TPU 8t and aimed at confidential training and running of AI models. Google said in a blog post that it builds security into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected even while in use. It also has a custom inferencing network that lets it run reasoning alongside training. Google says this lets companies train small models on their own data without moving it between devices.

The TPU 8i Max effectively joins two of the inference-focused TPU 8i chips from April in one package. That doubles memory capacity, processing power and bandwidth, so models can handle a wider range of information in a query.

TechCrunch notes that Microsoft, Amazon, OpenAI and Anthropic are also developing their own AI chips to reduce dependence on Nvidia. It adds that the launch comes at a vulnerable moment for Nvidia, whose chief executive admitted over the weekend to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

stories.title: N-able takes its remote access service offline after researcher publishes zero-days
stories.deck: The company pulled its hosted N-Central product and told self-hosting customers to shut theirs down after dozens of vulnerabilities appeared online.
summary: N-able has taken its cloud-hosted N-Central service offline after security flaws were published online with no advance notice to the company, TechCrunch reported on 10 November. In a status update, N-able said the hosted service would stay down while it secures the environments and carries out remediation.

The company also urged customers who run N-Central on their own servers to take those deployments down, fearing attackers could use the public exploits to break into customer networks. N-Central lets corporate customers remotely access and manage other devices and systems on the same network, so users cannot rely on it during the outage. TechCrunch noted that remote access tools are frequent hacker targets because they can give wide access to a company's network and internal data.

Security researcher Ben Bales posted the "zero-day" bugs on GitHub on Sunday. On X he called them Able2Shell and described them as a mix of flaws that can steal credentials, create new administrator accounts and gain root access to affected N-able systems. He told Bleeping Computer he released them because the company had allegedly failed to patch flaws he reported in a different product. That is his account; N-able's response to it is not given in TechCrunch's report.
N-able said it has no evidence that any customer environment was successfully attacked. A spokesperson did not say whether the company is able to check, for example through server logs.

stories.title: Australia to introduce mandatory reporting after OpenAI hack
stories.deck: The government accepted all 18 recommendations of a rapid review into an OpenAI agent's access to Medicare systems, and plans a new AI safety regulator.
summary: Australia will create an AI safety regulator and require AI companies to notify the government quickly of serious incidents, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced on Tuesday 10 November, according to Guardian Australia. The move follows a June incident in which an AI agent developed by OpenAI accessed data from Services Australia and three other systems. OpenAI became aware in August but did not tell the government until mid-September.

Albanese released the recommendations of a rapid review, though not its findings or report, which he promised to publish later. He said the government accepts all 18 recommendations. Agencies are asked to consider a "failure to prevent" offence, which would criminalise developing an AI model that causes harm without reasonable steps to stop it. The six planned obligations include security controls, risk management, rapid incident notification and independent evaluation of models.

Home affairs minister Tony Burke said it should never be arguable that someone "didn't know the computer was loaded". Albanese called the breach "minor" for personal privacy, saying no personal details were obtained, and Guardian Australia understands OpenAI is unlikely to face further legal proceedings.

Reactions split. AI researcher Toby Walsh said company leaders should be criminally liable. Greens leader David Shoebridge called the plan a "capitulation" because it only asks the government to "consider" tougher steps. The Coalition backed it. OpenAI said it is reviewing the proposals.

stories.title: Blackstone to invest Rs 5,000 crore for 16% stake in IIFL Finance
stories.deck: The private equity giant is part of a Rs 6,414 crore fresh equity raise by the listed lender, which plans to expand gold and other secured lending.
summary: Blackstone will put Rs 5,000 crore into IIFL Finance for roughly a 16% stake, The Indian Express reported on 10 November. The money is part of a Rs 6,414 crore primary equity raise by the listed non-banking finance company. Promoters Nirmal Jain and R Venkataraman will invest Rs 1,264 crore and Anchorage Capital Rs 150 crore. All of it will go into the company as fresh capital.

IIFL's board approved the deal on Tuesday as a preferential issue. Blackstone will invest through compulsorily convertible preference shares, which turn into equity at Rs 602 each within 18 months of allotment, while the promoters will subscribe to preferential warrants. The report puts IIFL Finance's market capitalisation at Rs 26,746 crore.

The infusion is expected to lift the company's capital adequacy ratio from about 17% to about 30% on a pro forma basis as of September 2026. The report says that should support expansion, better credit ratings and lower borrowing costs over time. IIFL plans to use the funds to grow secured lending, especially gold finance, and expects to draw on Blackstone's expertise in technology, data analytics and artificial intelligence. Blackstone representatives are proposed to join the board.

Jain called the investment a strong endorsement of the franchise, and said it gives headroom to expand while keeping discipline on risk and capital. Mukesh Mehta of Blackstone called IIFL a leading retail lending platform. Jain and Venkataraman will remain co-promoters.

stories.title: US inflation higher than expected in October
stories.deck: Prices rose 0.4% on the month, above analyst forecasts, strengthening the case for a Federal Reserve rate rise in December.
summary: US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, faster than the 0.3% analysts had expected, according to official figures reported by the BBC on 10 November. The monthly rise was lower than September's 0.6%. The figures arrived a week after midterm elections that were fought over cost-of-living pressures.

The BBC said the increase was driven by housing, food and energy costs. Energy prices rose 0.7% in October, far less than the 5.2% jump in September. The BBC adds that crude oil traded at just over $70 a barrel before the US-Israel war with Iran began and is now above $100. The Bureau of Labor Statistics could not give the usual 12-month figure because it did not collect data in October 2025. For the 12 months to September, inflation was 3.7%.

Analysts quoted by the BBC say the higher-than-expected reading raises the chance that the Federal Reserve raises interest rates at its December meeting. Fed governor Christopher Waller, speaking before the data came out, also indicated he was leaning towards an increase in December even if October's figures were softer than expected.

The BBC also pointed to tariffs as a factor, citing New York Fed research that found US businesses absorbed nearly 90% of the cost of added tariffs, and that each percentage point rise in average tariffs raised consumer goods prices by nearly 0.25% after a year.

stories.title: Bank of England's inflation response 'risks higher rates for longer'
stories.deck: Thinktank Niesr says last week's quarter-point rise was too timid and could leave inflation above target until at least 2030.
summary: The Bank of England risks keeping interest rates higher for longer after a hesitant response to rising inflation, according to the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (Niesr), as reported by the Guardian on 11 November. The thinktank said last week's quarter-point rise, from 3.75% to 4%, is likely to leave inflation above the Bank's 2% target until at least 2030 unless tougher action follows. The Bank's committee also hinted at another increase.

Niesr director David Aikman said inflation is set to pass 4% in the new year, just as most 2027 pay awards are being agreed, raising the risk that it becomes embedded. He argued one more quarter-point rise is unlikely to be enough and that waiting will force the committee to do more later. UK inflation is currently 3.5%, pushed up by fuel costs since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran at the end of February.

Brent crude, persistently above $100 a barrel recently against about $70 before the war, briefly fell below $90 on Tuesday after Donald Trump downplayed the need for military action against Iran. Niesr's forecasts assume $105 oil, and it cautioned that shipping and refining problems mean consumer prices will fall slowly. Economist Stephen Millard said the lower price depends on Trump sticking to his stance.
Niesr expects UK growth of 1.6% this year but 0.9% in 2028 and criticised the chancellor for deferring hard budget decisions.

stories.title: Sonia Gandhi's memoir 'Belonging' sparks political row
stories.deck: Claims in the Congress leader's new book have drawn sharp attacks from the BJP and a rebuttal from Pranab Mukherjee's daughter.
summary: Sonia Gandhi's memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, went on sale in India on Tuesday, 10 November, with an official launch likely on 16 November, The Hindu reported. Gandhi told The Guardian that Penguin Random House India dropped the book in August after she declined some edits; Penguin disputes that.

Several passages are her own account and have not been independently verified in the reports read. She writes that Pranab Mukherjee hinted in 2010 at a wish to become prime minister, which she says shocked her. His daughter Sharmistha Mukherjee replied on X that ambition is not a crime. She also writes of having "practically no real contact" with Narendra Modi. The BBC reports she describes saying "Theek hai" in 2004 before refusing the prime minister's post.

The BJP attacked the book on Tuesday, according to The Indian Express. Spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari said it revolves around a "Babri vote bank" and noted the Bofors scandal is missing. Spokesperson C R Kesavan accused her of whitewashing the Emergency. BJP leader H S Phoolka disputed her account of the Army's 1984 deployment, calling it contrary to facts.

Congress Rajya Sabha member Rajeev Shukla said the BJP was giving the book a political spin and asked that her sentiments be respected. AAP leader Saurabh Bharadwaj called her remorse over 1984 unverifiable hearsay, and JD(U)'s Sanjay Kumar Jha questioned her 2004 account. These are party positions.

stories.title: MEA slams US court summons to NSA Doval and ex-RAW chief Goel
stories.deck: New Delhi calls a civil suit by Khalistani figure Gurpatwant Singh Pannun frivolous, while sources describe the summons as routine.
summary: India's government on Tuesday dismissed a US court civil summons naming national security adviser Ajit Doval and former R&AW chief Samant Goel, calling it a "frivolous lawsuit" built on "fabricated and malicious" claims, according to The Times of India. The paper said the government also asserted that the legal manoeuvring by Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a designated Khalistani terrorist, has no merit.
External affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said requests to serve judicial documents in India can only be routed through the designated central authority, the ministry of law and justice.

The ministry's reaction followed reports that the US state department had informed India by diplomatic note of the suit, filed by Pannun, a member of Sikhs for Justice, over an alleged plot to assassinate him. The summons seeks damages and was delivered to the Indian embassy in Washington on 9 October, the report said. Unnamed sources described it as a routine, procedural step and noted that US courts have issued similar summonses before, including to Manmohan Singh in 2013 and Jiang Zemin in 2002. Both of those suits were eventually dismissed.

The report adds that the court order came ahead of the 20 November sentencing of Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national arrested by the US in the case. The state department note said its action followed court instructions and should not be read as a US position on the case or the merits of any claims.

stories.title: Ladakh hill council elections on December 4 amid boycott and protests
stories.deck: The first polls since six new districts were created will fill eight councils, but Kargil shut down in protest over holding them in winter.
summary: Ladakh will elect all eight of its Autonomous Hill Development Councils on 4 December, Chief Secretary Ashish Kundra announced in Leh on Tuesday, 10 November. With six new districts created this year, the councils will have 100 seats, up from 26 each in Leh and Kargil, and 36 are reserved for women for the first time. The Indian Express put the electorate at 1.87 lakh. Nominations close on 17 November, and the process is due to finish by 8 December.

Kargil observed a complete shutdown on Tuesday, called by the Kargil Democratic Alliance, which objects to the delimitation and to polling in harsh winter. Co-chairman Sajjad Kargili said around 25 percent of Ladakh's population would be outside the region, and spoke of "bureaucracy raj". The Ladakh Buddhist Association in Leh has announced a boycott of the panchayat and municipal polls, according to NDTV. Separately, Leh Apex Body co-chairman Tsering Dorjey Lakrook, backed those polls but called December a bad time for the council vote.

Kundra defended the schedule, saying schools stay open until mid-December, polling stations will have heaters and elderly voters will get separate queues. He said new councils would have January to March to prepare budgets and would keep their existing powers. Reports note that talks between the Centre and Ladakh groups on statehood and Sixth Schedule status stalled on 22 October. Panchayat and municipal polls are due on 21 November.

stories.title: Delhi post-Diwali pollution and CPCB data gaps
stories.deck: Firecrackers dominated Delhi's pollution a day after Diwali, while the pollution board defends its 500 AQI cap against private-app readings.
summary: Firecracker emissions made up more than 80 percent of Delhi's pollution load on Monday, 9 November, the day after Diwali, according to Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology models cited by The Times of India. Delhi's average AQI on Diwali, 8 November, was 376, the highest for the festival in five years. Air improved on Tuesday, with an AQI of 299 at 4pm, though it was 302 by 6pm. The India Meteorological Department credited favourable winds, and the paper said stubble burning was not a major contributor on Monday.

Questions arose because private apps showed readings far above the official figures. The Times of India said social media posts showed apps reporting 1,500 to 1,800 on Diwali night while the Central Pollution Control Board's figures stayed below 400. NDTV said some sites showed values above 1,000.

In a statement, the CPCB said the 500 ceiling is a deliberate design feature of the National Air Quality Index, in line with the US EPA scale, because anything above it stays in the 'Severe' category. It said the index uses calibrated 24-hour or 8-hour averages, while some apps draw on hourly readings from low-cost sensors. The board said short spikes such as firecracker bursts may appear as a data gap at a station, with those hours excluded from the daily average. It rejected under-reporting, attributing the differences to measurement and methodology. These are the board's own explanations; the reports did not include independent assessment.

stories.title: Supreme Court: onus on UP to ensure undertrials granted bail are released
stories.deck: The court said the state must not let prisoners stay jailed just because they cannot meet bail conditions.
summary: The Supreme Court has said the responsibility lies with Uttar Pradesh to ensure that undertrial prisoners granted bail are actually freed and do not stay in jail because they cannot meet release conditions such as bail bonds, cash security or local sureties, The Hindu reported on 10 November.

A bench headed by Justice M M Sundresh passed the order after learning that 264 undertrials were granted bail in only 20 of the state's 75 districts, yet just 158 were released. The other 106 remained in custody for various reasons, including being unable to provide financial security or a guarantor. Senior advocate Gaurav Aggarwal, the court's amicus curiae, said figures for the remaining 55 districts were not yet known. State counsel assured the court the needful would be done within a reasonable time.

The court said district legal services authorities should not turn away prisoners who have private lawyers but still cannot satisfy bail conditions, saying there cannot be any differentiation between the two groups. It said denying liberty to those a court has found deserving of bail, merely because they cannot afford the conditions, affects the right to life under Article 21. "The onus lies on the State to make sure that these persons are released from custody," the bench said.
The court asked trial courts to modify conditions suitably, said its order covers all 75 districts, and listed the suo motu case on bail policy for January 2027.

stories.title: First day of Ukraine peace talks constructive, Zelensky says
stories.deck: US-hosted talks between Kyiv, Moscow and Washington in Abu Dhabi ended their first day with cautious praise but no sign of a breakthrough.
summary: The first of two days of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the United States ended in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday after about four hours. Talks are expected to resume on Wednesday. President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was not in the room, said after being briefed by his negotiators that the format had been "constructive and quite substantive". US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking in Paris, called the meeting "very productive" but said a lot of work remained.

Delegates were tight-lipped. Zelensky said humanitarian issues, including prisoner exchanges and the return of children, were discussed, and that security guarantees were also on the agenda. Before the talks, a US official said Moscow and Kyiv were showing "a little bit of flexibility, privately" over who would control eastern Ukraine after the war, but that the territorial question could not be settled until a postwar security architecture was agreed.

Public positions remain far apart, the BBC reports. Moscow wants Ukraine to give up the parts of Donetsk it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the current line. Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said Moscow would not accept a ceasefire. Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko told the BBC he believed Donald Trump wanted "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine"; that is his opinion.
Fighting continued meanwhile. Ukraine's prime minister said Russia hit five major energy substations overnight, per the Guardian's live coverage. Both reports date from 10 November.

stories.title: Israel's new parliament sworn in as leaders compete to form government
stories.deck: Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has the first chance to oust Benjamin Netanyahu, but neither side has a majority.
summary: Israel's new Knesset was sworn in on Tuesday, with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot trying to replace caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the BBC reported. The former army chief was asked to form a government by President Isaac Herzog on Sunday, after 67 of the 120 members backed him against 46 for Netanyahu.

The arithmetic is hard. Eisenkot's bloc of four parties won 48 seats in last month's election, against 53 for Netanyahu's bloc, so neither can govern alone. Eisenkot has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension. Netanyahu stays as caretaker meanwhile.

Arab-led parties may hold the balance of power. The United Arab List and the Joint List won 19 seats between them, a record. Netanyahu has ruled out working with them, and three parties in Eisenkot's bloc oppose including them. The United Arab List says it would join an Eisenkot-led coalition, while the Joint List has offered outside support.

Eisenkot has called for a "national emergency government" open to any party accepting four principles, including equal national service for all and recognising Hamas as a terrorist organisation. The BBC notes these could be obstacles for ultra-Orthodox and Arab parties. Netanyahu, in a video on Monday, called for a unity government under his leadership and warned against relying on "the Islamists", an apparent reference to Arab parties. This account rests on one BBC report.

stories.title: Federal judge allows Trump's $10bn defamation lawsuit against BBC to proceed
stories.deck: A Florida judge partly denied the broadcaster's bid to dismiss the case over a Panorama edit, though Trump must still prove his claims.
summary: A federal judge in Florida ruled on Tuesday that Donald Trump's $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC can go ahead, partly denying the broadcaster's motion to dismiss, the Guardian reported. The case concerns a Panorama documentary, Trump: A Second Chance, which joined together separate remarks he made before the 6 January Capitol attack.

Judge Jeffrey T Kuntz, who was appointed by Trump, wrote that the edit joined comments nearly 55 minutes apart and "may independently establish the plausibility of actual malice". He rejected the BBC's argument that this was ordinary editing to shorten a seventy-minute speech, saying it created "something different than what was stated in the speech". These are the judge's findings at the pleading stage, taking Trump's allegations as true.

The ruling was not a clean win for Trump. The judge dismissed his claim under Florida's Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act, and said Trump must prove actual malice at trial and show actual damages.

The BBC said it was surprised but respected the court's authority, remained confident in its position, and would keep responding through the legal process. Trump called the ruling a "huge victory" on Truth Social. This account relies on a single Guardian report, published early on 11 November.

stories.title: Formula 1 season to finish in Qatar and Abu Dhabi as planned
stories.deck: F1 has stood Imola down as a back-up, but says it will cancel the Middle East races if the Iran conflict worsens.
summary: Formula 1 has told Italy's Imola circuit it will not be needed as a back-up for the final two races of the 2026 season, which remain scheduled for Qatar on 27-29 November and Abu Dhabi on 4-6 December. The BBC reported the decision on Tuesday, 10 November, which Autosport says was F1's deadline for giving Imola an answer.

F1 says it chose to press ahead because the situation in the two countries has not "negatively developed" in recent months. It cites government travel advice that still allows travel, valid insurance, events going ahead and business back at normal levels. A spokesperson said that if things worsen before the races, F1 "will not hesitate to do the right thing", with safety the priority. Autosport notes that this leaves no plan B if the war escalates.

The conflict began in late February when the United States and Israel struck Iran. It has already disrupted the calendar: the Saudi Arabian race was cancelled, and the Bahrain race was postponed and eventually held in Malaysia in October. MotoGP ran its Qatar round last weekend.

Not everyone is comfortable. The BBC says several senior F1 figures voiced disquiet privately, as both venues are near areas of the Strait of Hormuz where missile strikes continue. Team bosses quoted by Autosport say they trust F1 and the FIA; Ferrari's Fred Vasseur said he wants to race wherever told.

stories.title: Noskova beats Gauff to reach WTA Finals semi-finals
stories.deck: The Wimbledon champion became the first player into the last four on her debut at the season-ending event.
summary: Linda Noskova beat Coco Gauff 6-3 6-3 at the WTA Finals to become the first player to reach the semi-finals, BBC Sport reported. The 21-year-old Czech, the Wimbledon champion, is making her debut at the tournament and sealed the win with an ace.

Noskova, the world number eight, broke Gauff's serve four times in the first set alone and made only one unforced error in a dominant second. The BBC described her play as controlled aggression, with powerful winners that outmuscled one of the tour's best movers. It was her sixth win over a top-10 player this season. Afterwards she joked that the crowd's cheers were "a little weaker in the match" and said she felt she stayed in it from start to finish.

Gauff, ranked fourth, struggled on serve. She hit eight aces and eight double faults and won only six of 24 points behind her second serve. She won a thriller against fellow American Jessica Pegula on Sunday, and can still qualify for the last four, as can Pegula.

In the other group-one match reported, Pegula beat alternate Marta Kostyuk 6-2 7-5, her first win since September. Kostyuk, who has had a wrist injury since August, learned on Saturday that she would play after world number one Elena Rybakina withdrew. Pegula made five unforced errors to Kostyuk's 17, though the second set saw four breaks of serve before Pegula broke at 5-5 and served out the win.

stories.title: Vaishali Rameshbabu sees Total Chess as training for World Championship
stories.deck: The Indian grandmaster opened with a blitz win over Hans Niemann and says facing strong men in Budapest will sharpen her for Ju Wenjun.
summary: Vaishali Rameshbabu began her Total Chess pilot event campaign in Budapest late on Tuesday by beating Hans Niemann in a blitz game, The Indian Express reported. The 24-player field includes only two women, Vaishali and Bibisara Assaubayeva, and the main tournament starts on Wednesday. The paper's writer attended at the invitation of Total Chess.

In an interview before the blitz section, Vaishali said she sees the event as training for her Women's World Chess Championship match against reigning champion Ju Wenjun. She expects a daily challenge against strong opponents in any format.

She contrasted this preparation with the Candidates, where she had to face seven players in a double round-robin; now she thinks about one opponent at a time. She said she has not yet felt herself becoming her rival, as Garry Kasparov once described of Anatoly Karpov, but suggested that might come closer to the match.

On playing men, she said years of Grand Prix and women's events left little room for Open tournaments, but that those events test a player until the last move, and the men here are very strong. She said she still works with a psychologist, whose name she keeps private. Training hours matter less than being in good shape, she said: 12-13 hours is pointless if the brain is not working well.
